blocks.text: Oxides of nitrogen are NO, N₂O, NO₂, N₂O₄ and N₂O₅ in which oxidation states range from I+ to V+. N₂O₄ and N₂O₅ decay quickly to other oxides. NO and NO₂ are collectively called as NOₓ. The structures, properties and uses of these oxides are given in Table 12.2.

blocks.caption: Table 12.2 Properties of some common oxides of nitrogen
rows: Nitrous oxide/ Nitrogen oxide (Laughing gas) N₂O
Colourless gas, water-soluble, neutral, sweet smelling, helps in combustion
Dental anaesthetic, propellant for whipped ice cream, synthesis of NaN₃
Nitric oxide, Nitrogen dioxide NO, N₂O₂
Colourless gas, slightly water-soluble, neutral, NO is paramagnetic while N₂O₂ is diamagnetic, oxidising as well as reducing in nature
Biochemical messenger (Lowers blood pressure and role in other body functions), synthesis of nitrosyl carbonyls
Nitrogen dioxide/Nitrogen peroxide, Nitrogen tetraoxide NO₂, N₂O₄; 2NO₂ (Brown) ⇌ N₂O₄ (Colourless): Cool →, ← Heat
NO₂ is a reddish-brown gas, paramagnetic, and reacts with water to form HNO₃ and HNO₂, N₂O₄ is colourless liquid or solid
Rocket propellant, HNO₃ formation by Ostwald process, explosives

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: NO is nitric oxide (nitrogen monoxide), not nitrogen dioxide; nitrogen dioxide is NO₂, in the next row. N₂O₂ is the dimer of NO.

blocks.alt: Electron-dot structures from the Structure column of Table 12.2. N2O: N≡N–O with a lone pair on the end N and three lone pairs on O. NO: N=O with a lone pair and one unpaired electron on N and two lone pairs on O. N2O2: O=N–N=O with a lone pair on each N and two on each O. NO2: O–N=O with one unpaired electron on N. N2O4: two NO2 units joined by an N–N bond, each N with one N–O and one N=O bond.
blocks.caption: Table 12.2: Properties of some common oxides of nitrogen, Structure column (original drawing after the structures printed in the textbook's Table 12.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Table 12.2 prints NO as :N≡O: (a triple bond with only 10 electrons), which does not fit the table's own statement that NO is paramagnetic. NO has 11 valence electrons: N=O with an unpaired electron on N, as drawn above.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Another recommended name for ammonia by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) is Azane and for ammonium is Azanium. These names have been derived from Azote, a Greek name for nitrogen, meaning “no life”. These names are used in naming derivatives of ammonia and ammonium e.g. sodium azide (NaN₃).
